items.title: Editing Empathy: How Christopher White, ACE, Shaped 'American Doctor'
items.summary: When director Poh Si Teng began following three American physicians into Gaza, she captured an unfiltered look at healthcare workers operating under extraordinary conditions inside a warzone. But how can you take that powerful footage and translate it into a documentary? Enter veteran editor Christopher White, ACE. He took over the edit from Ema Ryan Yamazaki and later collaborated with her across a 12-hour time difference between New York and Tokyo. We spoke with Christopher White about the emotional challenges of working with sensitive footage, the mechanics of balancing three distinct character arcs without a script, and how a global tag-team edit brought this essential story to life. Let's dive in. - YouTubewww.youtube.com NFS: Hi Christopher! Could you begin by telling us how you got involved with American Doctor? Christopher White: Ema Ryan Yamazaki was the first editor on this film. She started in February of 2025. At that stage, the director Poh Si Teng had only started following the doctors with her camera the month before. So there wasn’t much footage to work with, and it wasn’t certain what type of film this could be…a short, a feature? Ema encouraged Poh to keep filming if she wanted it to be a feature, which Poh did. But Ema’s schedule only allowed her to work through April. It was then that I came on board to carry the project through the summer and fall. Poh continued filming for several more months, and it became clear that there was enough footage and story to aim for a feature-length film. NFS: How did the project challenge your existing understanding of its subject matter? CW: The project was challenging for me because I felt I didn't know enough about the circumstances in Gaza. I was definitely in over my head at the start of this edit, which is fine with me. I often choose projects based on what I don’t know, but want to know more about. items.title: Stada 2.0 is Live: Here’s What You Need to Know About This Next-Gen Remote Storage Platform
items.summary: Since its launch in 2023 by brothers Michael Cioni and Peter Cioni, who worked at notable companies such as Frame.io and Netflix, Strada has been one of the more intriguing brands in the collaborative remote storage space. And while it might be hard to imagine now, before the AI revolution swept all of film and video technology into a vacuum, cloud storage was the big topic, hotly debated and viewed as the future. Strada has quietly continued on this path to find a way to connect teams without the expensive, slow file transfer speeds that usually come with cloud storage. Let’s look at Strada 2.0, which is live now and is promised to be a new platform for video editors, filmmakers, and creative professionals looking for fast, secure, and cost-effective access to large files—without constantly uploading everything to the cloud. What is Strada, Again? So, as mentioned above, Strada has been around for several years now and, thanks to its 'founders' combined pedigree, it quickly became a major brand in the remote storage space almost immediately after its launch. Still, if you aren’t super familiar with the company and what it offers, this explainer video from the brand does a good job of catching any interested viewer up. Hosted by Michael Cioni, who, if you’ve ever wandered the halls of a film and video tech trade show like NAB, you’ve likely encountered as he’s been a dynamic spokesperson, as he was with his role with Frame.io before. Basically though, Strada offers the following capabilities: Transform your on-premises storage & computers into a global peer-to-peer video network Enable instant video editing with lightning-fast access to remote files Save time, reduce costs, and eliminate dependence on traditional cloud services Collaborate seamlessly with your team — no matter where they are in the world The goal is to be more than just basic storage software, but a holistic collaboration platform for entire post-production teams. items.title: The Future of Smartphone Cameras is Here With the ARRI x HONOR Robot Phone
items.summary: Well, after months of teasers and reporting, that weird ARRI x HONOR Robot Phone camera thing is now officially alive—in China at least. The companies have issued press releases announcing that the HONOR Robot Phone is now officially available, which they celebrate as the mobile debut of ARRI Image Science and HONOR’s gimbal camera technology. Set to be a “new species of smartphone” that integrates key elements of ARRI Image Science and carries a “co-engineered” credit, the HONOR Robot Phone is fully debuted with a range of mobile imaging, AI, and robotic camera technologies and with ARRI LogC3, ARRI Wide Gamut 3, and ARRI Looks. Let’s check it out. The ARRI x HONOR Robot Phone To be honest, when it was first announced, this product confused us as it’s certainly unique. Set to basically be a smartphone with a built-in gimbal camera, or a gimbal camera with a built-in smartphone, depending on how you look at it, this is a product that is unlike any we’ve seen before. “The HONOR Robot Phone is an important milestone in ARRI’s expansion into Content Creation. Together with HONOR, we are translating ARRI’s perspective on image quality, color, and visual storytelling into a new category. This gives more creators access to greater creative control and a stronger connection between capture and post-production.” — David Bermbach, Chief Product Officer of ARRI. And while we’ll likely have much more to say and explore with it now that it’s officially launched and set to be available to users and reviewers, in China at least, it’s also undeniably a bold step for both companies, with ARRI’s work here being the most interesting part. The HONOR Robot Phone Features So, you can judge for yourself based on many demos and featurettes already put out by the company, but it’s safe to say that this new robot phone will at least try to offer some new features that haven’t been seen in this type of setup. items.title: Roku Created a New Channel That's Only AI Slop 24/7
items.summary: Tired of not being able to decide what to watch on TV? What if you just turned your brain completely off and let AI feed slop through your eyeballs and into your frontal cortex non-stop 24/7? That may sound like the obese future from Wall-E, but I have to inform you it is already here. Last week, The Roku Channel launched Fairground AI, a 24/7 channel that runs entirely on AI-generated content. You get a nice mix of narrative shorts and commercials, all created for humans by our AI overlords. It's the kind of mind-numbing stuff they forced Alex DeLarge to sit through in A Clockwork Orange, and now you have access to it in your own home. Let's dive in. - YouTubewww.youtube.com Does Anyone Actually Want This? This is so interesting because I am not just using my Hollywood brain here; I have no idea who in the Western world wants to watch this stuff. Every trend we see is people watching their old favorite shows over and over again or comfort movies. But that doesn't account for Roku's plans to go global, or, at least, go far East to a market that dwarves America. China’s short-form video ecosystem is currently undergoing a massive, AI-driven pivot: Mass Production: More than 95% of the ~128,000 microdramas released in China last quarter were AI. Explosive Viewership: In January, AI-generated short-form dramas captured 38% of the top 100 hits (up from just 7% a year prior), pulling in an astounding 2.55 billion views. Synthetic Superstars: The Tilly Norwoods of China, "Qin Ling Yue" and "Lin Xi Yan" are already set to star in 60+ shorts. The Future of the Living Room Screen Is the West destined for what the East already views as commonplace? Founder & CEO of Fairground Entertainment Colin Petrie-Norris said of the new Roku deal, “Cable and linear TV was the realm of the very well-financed. items.title: Stop Trying to Decode Christopher Nolan’s Movies While Watching Them
items.summary: Let me know if you feel the same, but I have trouble watching many movies. As a writer, I am frequently engaging on a craft level, even with new films. It's very rare that I enjoy a movie so much that it sweeps me off my feet and takes me out of my analytical brain and into my entertainment one. And I have to admit, this happens a lot to me with Nolan. Because I know he's a masterful craftsman, I start picking apart every scene as I go. And it's my fault when I wind up having to see his movies a few times to tell if I really like them. But in my defense, Christopher Nolan is famous for constructing narrative puzzles. And I like working them out, although the director thinks I should just shut up and watch...Which I kind of agree with. In a candid clip, Nolan told people like me to just enjoy the movie. "It's my job as a writer-director particularly to try and be the audience for the film as I'm writing them. People who really try and understand the structure or analyze it as they're watching it tend to get very frustrated with it and dislike the film intensely. People who kind of just let it wash over them—which is more the way I'm intending it—they tend to sort of get it the way I intended it a little bit more." Christopher Nolan’s Response to Making Complicated Movies #shorts #dunkirk #christophernolan youtube.com Feeling Over Decoding Okay, I have to admit, I feel targeted by that Nolan comment, but he is right; I do wind up loving most of his movies the second time they wash over me, and I have released all my anxieties about what's happening. I have to say, the first movie I watched as an audience member was Oppenheimer, which just blew me out of the water. For Nolan, the goal isn't to force the viewer into an academic exercise in real time; it's to get them out of their own heads and entertained.
